extracted.intended_audience: homeowners, builders, and small-scale sanitary engineers designing sewage systems for single houses
extracted.subtask_description: Practical design and operation guidance for plumbing fixtures and sewage disposal systems serving a single house, including traps, water-closets, flushing supplies, land treatment (surface, artificial beds, subsurface tile), sedimentation tanks, and dosing mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trap necessity and seal depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Traps themselves are essential, and great care should be taken to see that each trap is in place and has a seal of the depth already mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every fixture has a properly installed trap with the recommended seal depth. Traps prevent sewer gas entry and must be checked for presence and correct seal depth regularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trap type: simplest trap preferred (plain S trap)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best trap to use in any fixture is the simplest, and a plain S trap answers every purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simple trap designs over complicated types. Simpler traps are less likely to fail and are adequate for typical household use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trap clean-out provision
rubrics_metrics.description: It is always wise to have a clean-out at the bottom of the trap; that is, a small opening which can be closed with a screw plug, so that when the trap becomes clogged, it can be easily opened and cleaned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a screw-plug clean-out at the trap bottom to allow easy maintenance and unclogging without dismantling the trap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vent-pipes are generally unnecessary for preventing trap depletion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vent-pipes were formerly insisted upon because of the feeling that a large amount of water down the soil-pipe might induce suction to draw out trap water; experiments have shown it is practically impossible to draw off the water from a trap in this way, and the system of vent-pipes does little more than add to the cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add vent-pipe systems solely to prevent trap siphonage for single-house installations; they add cost and offer little practical benefit according to experiments cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-closet selection criteria (Maine State Board of Health)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of a water-closet should be made from those which have the bowl and trap all in one piece, which are simple in construction, are self-cleansing, and have a safe water-seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable types listed: short-hopper, washout, washdown, syphonic, and syphon-jet. Prefer models with integrated bowl+trap, simplicity, self-cleansing action, and reliable water-seal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pan-closets and long-hopper closets
rubrics_metrics.description: The old-fashioned pan-closet becomes easily clogged, allows matter to decompose in the receptacle under the valve... and, in spite of its being cheaper, should not be used. The long-hopper closet is also objectionable, for the same reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not install pan or long-hopper closets due to clogging and decomposition issues even if they are cheaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washout vs washdown evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The washout closet has too shallow a pool of water to receive the soil, and the trap below and the portion above the trap do not receive a sufficient scouring from the flush. The washdown closet, having a deep basin, a deep water-seal, smaller surfaces uncovered by water, and a more efficient scouring action, is more cleanly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer washdown (an improved short-hopper) over washout designs because of deeper basin and better scouring; avoid washout where scouring is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syphonic and syphon-jet closets preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Syphonic closets use a contracted outlet to form a syphon on flushing; syphon-jet closets add a jet to help drive contents rapidly. These two closets are preferable to those of any other style and are more nearly noiseless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, choose syphonic or syphon-jet closets for superior flushing force, retention of an adequate trap seal after flush, and quieter operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flushing connection: avoid direct connection to small house supply
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be quite possible to connect directly to the closet rim where the flush enters, but objections: low pressure while other fixtures draw water may cause air to be drawn into the pipe; direct connection might conceivably allow filth to be drawn up into the water-pipe under certain conditions; small house pipes may not deliver water fast enough for effective flushing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid direct connection of water-closet flush to small house supply unless pressure is reliable. Consider other methods to ensure adequate flushing and prevent back-siphonage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flush tank for water-closet: copper-lined wooden tank (~3 gallons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly put in, just back of or above the closet, a small copper-lined wooden tank which holds about three gallons and can be discharged rapidly through a 1¼-inch pipe. This tank with fittings costs about $10 and allows rapid discharge while refilling slowly by float valve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a small local flush tank when house piping cannot deliver the needed rapid discharge; include float valve for automatic refill. Consider cost/necessity for each installation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic shut-off bibb for direct connection when pressure adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: If the house has a tank supply or if the pressure is strong enough to insure a positive flow at all times, there can be no objection... An automatic shut-off bibb would then be used on the water-pipe, allowing the water to flow freely as long as the bibb was opened, but closing automatically when released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where direct connection is acceptable (strong, reliable pressure), install an automatic shut-off bibb to allow free flow while open and automatic closure when released.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental principle: distribute organic matter to surface soil for bacterial action
rubrics_metrics.description: The first fundamental principle of sewage disposal is to distribute the organic matter in the sewage so that bacteria in the surface soil may most rapidly and thoroughly accomplish decomposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems (surface irrigation, artificial beds, subsurface tile) to place sewage where soil bacteria and air access (top ~12 inches) can act; avoid methods that prevent bacterial aerobic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three essential factors for land treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The three principles which will avoid 'sewage-sick' conditions are: plenty of air, presence of bacteria normally found in the surface layers of the soil, and intermittency of application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure designs promote aeration, use surface/topsoil bacterial activity, and apply sewage intermittently (rest periods) rather than continuous dosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid discharging sewage into streams used or potentially used for drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Discharging sewage into streams can carry pathogenic bacteria for hundreds of miles and cause epidemics; many states prohibit discharge from single houses into streams used for drinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discharge household sewage into streams that are or may be used for drinking water. Follow local statutes and public-health considerations; only discharge into large rivers/lakes where drinking use is not affected and law permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface application / irrigation sizing and rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sewage may be brought to the upper edge of a small piece of ground (grass) and allowed to run over the surface. Alternate plots so sewage is turned from one to another every day: each plot has one day's application and one day's rest. For a family of 10 persons using 25 gallons/day the total area provided should be one tenth of one acre, or an area seventy feet square divided into three plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide intermittent rotation of plots (three plots recommended); reserve one plot for winter/rainy season limitations; plan total area based on occupants and soil—example: one acre per 40 persons on worked loam over clay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface application for vegetable beds
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead sewage in channels between narrow beds about 8 feet wide with two rows of root crops; intermittent application essential; three beds should be provided as before; generally no provision needed for lower-end carry-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using for crops, maintain intermittent dosing, proper bed preparation (plowing/back-furrowing), and avoid overly clayey soils unless improved by sewage over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil suitability: clay and peaty soils limitations; sand advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Clay soils and peaty soils are useless for sewage disposal unless a few inches of cultivated topsoil exist; sandy soils absorb more water than clay and ideal coarse sand greatly increases purification rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess soil type before selecting method. If clay/peat, either improve with topsoil or use other methods; prefer coarse sandy material for artificial beds when high rate of discharge is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial sewage beds: sand specifications, capacity, and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Best material is coarse sand whose particles will not pass 60-mesh but will pass 10-mesh; such sand will purify at 50,000 gallons per acre per day. Beds are about 3 feet deep with light concrete side walls and bottom; divide bed into three parts and alternate weekly; in winter furrow beds to protect sewage from freezing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct artificial sand beds ~3 ft thick with concrete walls/bottom. Size beds by occupancy (about 50 sq ft per person with ideal sand). Apply sewage intermittently (bucketful doses) rather than continuous trickle; use furrows in winter and shift beds roughly weekly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rate / area per person for ideal sand bed
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal sand purifies sewage at 50,000 gallons per acre per day, implying about 50 square feet per person; a family of 10 persons could have all sewage taken care of on an area 25 feet square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 50 sq ft/person as a design guide for artificial sand beds; adjust for actual sand quality and intermittency practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsurface tile disposal: grade and length guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Grade must be adjusted to porosity: in fairly good sandy loam a proper grade is about 5 inches in 100 feet; the soil will absorb similar area as surface; usual allowance is about 40 feet of distribution pipe per person in well-cultivated soil (less for sandy). Lines of pipe should not be nearer than 10 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay tile at appropriate grade to ensure even distribution (steeper in gravelly soils, less in clay). Provide roughly 40 ft pipe/person (reduce for sandy soils). Space parallel lines ≥10 ft. Consider layout across slope to obtain desired grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of subsurface tile lines and prefer alternating beds
rubrics_metrics.description: Subdividing sewage among many short parallel lines makes proportionate distribution difficult; prefer to use not more than two lines, with the possibility of delivering sewage alternately to one or the other so one rests while the other acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design distribution with few long lines (≤2) and alternate dosing between them to maintain resting periods and avoid local overworking of soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid continuous trickling discharge on subsurface tile
rubrics_metrics.description: With small, constant trickling discharges the difficulty of distribution through long tile is gradually increased, and usually saturation of the soil occurs from joint to joint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement intermittent dosing (automatic syphon or manual valve) rather than continuous trickle to prevent progressive saturation and failure of tile distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic syphon for intermittent dosing
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'automatic syphon' chamber on the pipe line compresses air and then suddenly starts a syphon to discharge the chamber. The syphon chamber for a single house usually holds about one hour's flow and will discharge every ~60 minutes; cost about $12 delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install an automatic syphon or equivalent dosing device to provide intermittent doses to beds/pipes. Size the chamber to hold ~one hour's flow (approx. one-quarter of daily flow for dosing tank). Provide an overflow pipe in case valve/syphon is not actuated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual intermittent dosing alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermittent discharge may be made by a hand valve leading out from the chamber, where an attendant pulls the valve each hour or several times a day to discharge; an overflow pipe should be provided so sewage will still find its way if the valve is forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where automatic syphons are not used, provide a manual valve and clear operating schedule; include overflow safeguard to avoid spillage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedimentation tanks: remove solids and sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedimentation tanks remove solids before land treatment. Tanks should have capacity equal to about one day's flow for single-house sewage; e.g., ten persons at 25 gal/day need ~250 gal (33 cu ft) so suggested tank about 3 ft wide × 3 ft deep × 5 ft long. Tanks larger than necessary often reduce accumulated solids over time so infrequent cleaning is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a settling tank sized for ~one day's flow per household; allows solids to settle and reduces clogging of beds/tile. Expect possible intervals of a year or two between cleanings if sized correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedimentation tank inlet/outlet arrangement to avoid scum/sediment carry-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach an elbow to the entering pipe so sewage enters about halfway between top and bottom; similarly at the outlet or weir an elbow should take off liquid halfway between top and bottom so floating scum and bottom sediment are not carried away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design inlet and outlet so as to draw clarified liquid from mid-depth, minimizing carry-over of surface scum and bottom sludge to subsequent treatment beds or pipes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedimentation tank construction and ventilation notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tank must be built of concrete or masonry (timber not recommended). Walls may be 6 inches thick at top and 12–18 inches at bottom; bottom with 6 inches concrete; roof of flagstone or concrete slabs with wire mesh. Ventilation not necessary though an air-space above water helpful; tanks may smell initially but odors fade after months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use durable construction materials and adequate thickness for durability; allow an air gap above water but avoid ventilators that will broadcast early odors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete plant arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Full plant consists of the settling tank receiving raw sewage, discharging into a small dosing tank holding ~one hour's flow containing the automatic syphon, and the ground area (natural or artificial) which receives the intermittent discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems with staged treatment: sedimentation → dosing chamber with intermittent discharge → land treatment (surface/artificial/subsurface) sized and arranged per soil and occupancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underdrains: use only when groundwater interferes
rubrics_metrics.description: Underdrains are needed only where ground water comes up so high as to affect disposal (usually not needed unless groundwater within 3 feet of surface); in clay soils underdrain is not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install underdrains only when groundwater elevation threatens bed/tile function (within ~3 ft); avoid unnecessary expense if not required by site conditions.
